name: Eritai
world_status: accessible description is silent on stress

earlier_scan.note: Only comparative Lakes Plain works (Clouse 1997, Voorhoeve 1975) cited; no descriptive grammar or phonology of Eritai located.

new_statements.quote: [p.152] Tone is a prominent feature of all Lakes Plain languages and therefore was most likely a feature of some of the protolanguages as well. ... All the modern languages have at least high and low tone. [p.160] Although tonal contrast is found in virtually all of the the Lakes Plain languages, it will not be shown in the word list transcriptions. Additionally, stress is not marked because only a few original word lists marked it and it has not been found to be contrastive in any of the Lakes Plain languages to date. [p.162] Language: Eritai / Elicitor(s): D. Martin / Reliability: Obtained on survey. / Date: February 1985 / Village: Eri

The remainder of the languages also have combinations of high and low (or contours); Obokuitai has a fall (Jenison 1991)...' -- verbatim apart from the scanned 'modem'. (b) line 1327-1331 =…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Eritai, like all Lakes Plain languages, is tonal (at least high vs low tone); stress has not been found contrastive anywhere in the family. No source locates stress within the Eritai word. (For the closest sister lect Obokuitai, 75-76% cognate, Jenison & Jenison 1991 p.86 give a tone-dependent rule: final syllable if all pitches equal, otherwise the highest-pitched syllable, rightmost on ties; for Sikaritai, Martin 1991 p.93: last high-toned syllable, else first syllable.)
new_statements.secondary_stress: Nothing said for Eritai. (Martin 1991 p.92 for Sikaritai: one syllable per pause group carries an additional degree of stress.)
new_statements.domain_note: Family-level generalisation by a Lakes Plain fieldworker over survey word lists and colleagues' phonologies; the Eritai data behind it are a single 1985 survey word list (D. Martin, Eri village). Not a description of Eritai word prosody; the Obokuitai and Sikaritai rules quoted in rule_in_words are for different (though closely related) lects and are given for context only.
new_statements.identity_note: No description of Eritai (erit1239) itself exists. The quoted Clouse 1997 remarks are family-level (all Lakes Plain). Obokui village; 75-76% cognate with Eritai; Ethnologue: 'the dialect in Obogwi village is close, but not the same'), Martin 1991 = Sikaritai (sika1261; 50-55% cognate). 'Baburiwa' is an older cover label that Jenison & Jenison 1991 pp.69-70 say was applied to the speech of Obokui, Biri, Kustera and Haya together (i.e. Obokuitai + Biritai + Eritai); Ethnologue/Glottolog now reserve Baburiwa/Barua for Eritai [ert]. StressTyp's 'Obokuitai; Obogwitai; Baburiwa' entry is coded from the Obokuitai phonology and should not be read as an Eritai datum.

sources.citation: Jenison, D. Scott & Priscilla B. Jenison. 1991. Obokuitai phonology. In M. Hartzler & L. Wood (eds.), Workpapers in Indonesian Languages and Cultures 9, 69-90. Jayapura: Cenderawasih University & SIL.
sources.note: Describes OBOKUITAI (obok1239), the closest sister lect (75-76% lexical similarity), not Eritai. pp.69-70: Obokuitai speakers also live in 'Biri, Kustera, and Haya where related languages are spoken. The language of these groups was initially labeled "Baburiwa."' sec.5.4.2 Stress, p.86: 'Stress occurs on the last syllable of a word if the same pitch is on all syllables. In a word with various pitches, stress occurs on the highest pitch. In a word with two pitches of the same height which are the highest in the word, stress occurs on the syllable closest to the end of the word.' Two level pitc…

sources.citation: Martin, David L. 1991. Sikaritai phonology. In M. Hartzler & L. Wood (eds.), Workpapers in Indonesian Languages and Cultures 9, 91-120. Jayapura: Cenderawasih University & SIL.
sources.note: Describes SIKARITAI (55% cognate with Eritai), not Eritai; Martin is the elicitor of the 1985 Eritai survey list. sec.3 Stress group, p.93: 'A stress group consists of a group of 1-3 syllables... stress occurs on the last high tone or on the first syllable if there are no highs.' sec.2 p.92: pause group has one syllable with extra stress. sec.5.2: two tonemes, high and low. No mention of Eritai.
